blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Describing landscapes from photographs and images, adding geographical detail to maps, and using supporting material together with a map extract.

blocks.heading: Describing a photograph
blocks.text: A photograph is described from what it shows, organised from the foreground through the middle distance to the background, with the position words doing the organising. In the foreground, a flat field system with rectangular plots; in the middle distance, a steep slope under grass with a track climbing it; in the background, a flat-topped ridge against the sky. The description names landforms, vegetation, land use and buildings, with suitable geographical terms and simple adjectives. It adds nothing the photograph does not show, and it explains nothing either: features that cannot be pointed to in the image are invented, and reasons are explanation, which a describe question has not asked for.

blocks.heading: Adding detail to a map
blocks.text: Applying knowledge to a map means adding what the symbols imply. A weir on the river means a head of water, and a mill beside it means the head was used. Contours bending upstream in a V mark the valley the river has cut, so the flow direction is read off the Vs. Land use follows the relief, so the flat ground by the stream is the settlement's best land, and the inference is tied to the evidence on the sheet: each added detail names the symbol it comes from.

blocks.heading: Using material together
blocks.text: A map and a photograph read together let one source check the other: the photograph shows what the contour pattern means on the ground, and the map places what the photograph shows. A valley that looks broad in the image is measured on the map; a slope that looks steep on the sheet is checked against the photograph's horizon. Aerial photographs and satellite images extend the same skill, and a GIS layer, a data theme drawn over the base map, joins a distribution to the ground it lies on.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The photographs described here show the landforms of topics 2.2 and 2.3, and the map skills they sit with are the ones of the first two units of this topic.

blocks.heading: A photograph, described
blocks.text: A described photograph, worked from front to back. In the foreground: a dry stony river bed, a channel of rounded boulders and sand with no water in it. In the middle distance: flat open grazing land, tan and dusty, with a single dirt road running to the horizon and one windmill beside it. In the background: a line of low rocky hills, bare of vegetation on their upper slopes. The description uses the position words to organise it and names what is there, landforms, vegetation, land use and buildings, and it adds nothing: no farmer, no explanation, no crop the eye cannot see. The test is whether each thing named can be pointed to in the image.

blocks.heading: The invented photograph
blocks.text: The recorded error is adding features the photograph does not show, or explaining when a description is asked for. The correct move: describe only the visible, landforms, vegetation, land use, buildings, with position words doing the organising, and leave reasons for a question that asks for them. The test: can the feature be pointed to in the photograph, and does the question ask what or why?

blocks.heading: Two sources, one answer, worked
blocks.text: Supporting material beside a map, worked. A map extract shows a village on a river at a bridge; an accompanying photograph, taken from the bridge, shows the flood plain upstream under water after a storm. Read together: the map shows the village's site on the flat ground beside the river, and the photograph shows that flat ground flooded, so the joint conclusion is that the village stands on a flood plain that the river occupies after storms. Neither source carries the conclusion alone, the map has the site but not the hazard, the photograph the water but not the position, and using them together is the skill the syllabus names. Aerial photographs, satellite images and GIS layers extend the same pairing, one source checked against the other.

blocks.heading: Annotating a photograph, worked
blocks.text: Annotating, worked. Take the dry-riverbed photograph described earlier and add the geography the image implies, each label naming what it points at. The channel: a dry bed of rounded boulders, so the river flows after rain and not before it, an ephemeral channel. The boulders' rounding: worn in the wet season's flow, because angular rock rounds as it travels. The windmill in the middle distance: pumping groundwater for stock, so the grazing is ranched land, not wilderness. The bare upper slopes of the hills: too dry for cover, so the vegetation stops where the water does. Each annotation is a label the image supports, and the labels together are a field description written on the photograph itself, which is the technique's whole point.

blocks.heading: A map and photograph of one coast
blocks.text: The coastal extract and a photograph of the same shore, worked together. The map shows the cliff square, the bay with its sand beach, the headland with the beacon, and a photograph taken from the headland shows the cliff line falling to the bay in the middle distance and the hotel's promenade beyond. The joint reading places what the image shows, the cliff is the square 2174 edge, and confirms what the map draws, the beach is the flat strip in the bay, so a description of one can be checked against the other. Paper 2 pairs resources this way, and the skill is to use each for what it does best: the map for position and pattern, the photograph for texture and detail the map cannot hold.
